To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) construction phase GHG emissions should be included in the assessment of GHG mitigation strategies in the built environment; and 2) when construction phase emissions are included, it is impossible to achieve significant GHG mitigation through new residential construction.

the emissions from new low-energy residential development are underestimated when the temporal allocation is not included in the LCA, and the emissions from construction are underestimated if they are not allocated over the whole life span of the building.

the emissions from the construction phase of a residential building are more than double the emissions from all of the use-phase consumption activities, and the emissions from construction are so significant that the construction of new buildings should not be used as an instrument of carbon management.

a fundamental question of how to assess the GHG implications of new residential construction.

the following questions: How can city-level GHG management strategies be developed when the emissions from construction are not taken into account? the GHG implications of new residential developments are not understood as well as they should be.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, if we are to utilize new residential construction as an effective instrument of climate change adaptation and mitigation, we need to develop a new approach to city-level climate change management.
new residential construction is not a viable instrument for climate change mitigation in cities.

, when the GHG implications of new residential construction are understood wrongly, the instrument of low-energy construction may not be as useful in climate change mitigation as it is often assumed to be.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, when considering the role of new residential development as a climate change mitigation strategy, the temporal allocation of GHG emissions from the construction phase and the use phase needs to be considered in a holistic way.
, when the construction phase emissions are not properly accounted for, city-level GHG management may lead to the wrong conclusions and thus fail to produce effective mitigation strategies.
the emissions from new residential construction should be considered when planning for GHG reduction, but the city level is an inappropriate scale for the analysis.
